Way
WAY
n. (a road or path; a manner of life; the course God appoints; the earliest name for the Christian religion; rendering Hebrew derek, 'ōrach and Greek hodos)
From Old English weg, common Germanic, a road or course of travel; cognate with Latin via and with the verb to weigh in the older sense of carrying. Hebrew derek is built on a root meaning to tread, so the word literally names the track worn by feet — and the moral sense (a man's way, his habitual course) is the same word without change. Greek hodos is the road, and the compound methodos gives English method, a following-after along a road. Every biblical language uses the same word for the path underfoot and the life lived, and the metaphor is never dead.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Way in Scripture is the standard figure for the whole moral shape of a life, and the Bible knows only two of them. The first Psalm sets them side by side and ends with the LORD's knowledge of one and the perishing of the other: “the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Psa 1:6). Proverbs adds the warning that the difference is not obvious to the man walking it — “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Pro 14:12) — which is why the way must be revealed and not merely felt out. Isaiah promises a highway so plainly marked that the simple cannot lose it: “it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isa 35:8). The figure then collapses into a Person. The Lord Jesus does not say He teaches the way or shows it; He says “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). Accordingly the earliest name for the Christian religion in Acts is simply the Way (Act 9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14, 22) — not a doctrine to be held only, but a road to be walked.

Webster 1828 Definition

A road or path; by extension the course and manner of a life; in Scripture the two ways of righteousness and destruction, the way of holiness Isaiah foretold, Christ Himself as the only way to the Father, and the Way as the first name of the Christian religion.

WAY, n. [Sax. weg.] 1. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; hence, a road of any kind; a highway; a private road; a lane; a street.

2. Length of space; as a great way; a little way.

3. Course; direction of motion or travel. Which way did he go?

4. Manner of doing any thing; method; means; as, this is the way to be happy. In Scripture, the moral course of a life: “Teach me thy way, O Lord; I will walk in thy truth.” Ps. 86.

5. In Scripture, the ways of God are His providential dealings and His revealed precepts alike — “my ways [are] higher than your ways” (Isa 55:9) speaks of the former, “shew me thy ways, O LORD” (Psa 25:4) of the latter, and the two are never in conflict.

Key Scripture

Psa 1:6 — "For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish."

Pro 14:12 — "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death."

Isa 35:8 — "And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein."

Joh 14:6 — "Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me."

Modern Corruption

Religious pluralism recasts Joh 14:6 as one community's testimony rather than a universal claim, teaching that the ways are many and converge; and inside the church, “my walk” is reduced to a private inward experience with no defined road, no destination, and no obedience.

expand to see more

The pluralist correction of Joh 14:6 is now standard in mainline preaching and in progressive evangelicalism: Jesus is a way, or the way for Christians, and the several religions are so many roads up one mountain. The verse itself forbids the reading, and its second clause exists precisely to close the exit — no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. Peter says the same thing without metaphor (Act 4:12), and Paul stakes the entire mission on it: how shall they hear without a preacher? If the ways converged, the apostolic church wasted its blood. The exclusivity is not the church's arrogance; it is the confession that if a road had already run to the Father, the cross was a needless cruelty.

The domestic corruption is softer. “My walk with the Lord” has drifted into a term for interior mood — how one is feeling about God this month — detached from the commandments, the ordinances, the assembly, and any measurable direction. Scripture's figure is stubbornly external: a way has a surface underfoot, a direction, other travellers on it, and an end. Psalm 119 asks God to teach, incline, order, and quicken the psalmist's way, and every one of those requests is about what he will actually do. The recovery is plain: walk in the commandments, in the light, in love, in newness of life — all of them Pauline imperatives with feet in them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew derek (from a root meaning to tread — a trodden path, and so a manner of life) and 'ōrach (a track); Greek hodos (road, whence method), the term Acts uses absolutely for the Christian religion.

expand to see more

derek (Hebrew, H1870) — road, journey, manner of life; some seven hundred occurrences, and the same word carries the literal and moral senses without any shift, which is why Hebrew ethics is habitually described in travel language.

'ōrach (Hebrew, H734) — path, track; the poetic partner of derek, as in Psa 119:104 and the parallelism of Pro 4:18, “the path of the just is as the shining light.”

halak (Hebrew, H1980) — to walk; the verb that supplies the noun's force, and the root of later Jewish halakhah, the rule for walking; the New Testament's peripateō carries the same Hebrew idiom into Greek.

hodos (Greek, G3598) — road, way; used absolutely for the Christian religion at Act 9:2, 19:9, 19:23, 24:14 and 24:22, an idiom that presupposes Isaiah's highway of holiness.

The Two Ways — a teaching form running from Deu 30:15–19 and Psalm 1 through Mat 7:13–14 to the opening of the Didache; the oldest catechetical structure in Christian instruction and the frame for every Puritan treatise on the Christian walk.

Usage

"The Hebrew word for a moral course is the same word used for a dirt track. Biblical ethics is therefore never abstract: a man's way is where his feet have actually gone, and it can be read by anyone who follows the prints."

"Acts calls the church the Way five times before Christian appears once as an outsiders' nickname (Act 11:26). The self-designation the first believers used described a road they were on."

"Pro 14:12 is repeated verbatim at Pro 16:25 — a doubling in Hebrew idiom that marks the warning as fixed and certain, not a passing observation."
